beats.script_body: Dutch settlers landed here in 1623 and erected a battery of cannon to defend the pocket of land they called New Amsterdam — and it is from that battery of guns that the park takes its name. Today gardens, sculptures, memorials, monuments, and recreation areas fill the twenty-five acres of downtown's largest public space, with waterfront views of the Statue of Liberty across the harbor, and tugboats, barges, and sailboats working the water.

beats.script_body: The park is home to Castle Clinton National Monument, a fort built to defend against a British invasion in 1812. After the war, the round stone fort found a second life: it served as an immigration center before Ellis Island opened, and today it holds displays of historic Manhattan. It is also where you buy ferry tickets to the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island.

beats.script_body: For the more than twelve million immigrants who crossed the Atlantic between 1892 and 1954, the first glimpse of their new home was a one-hundred-and-sixty-five-foot copper woman, green from oxidation, holding a torch of liberty. Today the descendants of those immigrants account for nearly half the current population of the United States. Etched on the pedestal are the famous lines from Emma Lazarus's poem: "Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free."

beats.script_body: Since 1886 this statue — broken shackles at her feet and a tablet bearing the date of independence in her hand — has stood as an inspiration for Americans. A museum in the pedestal tells the story of sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi's creation, which was built with money donated by the French public and shipped across the Atlantic. The statue arrived in New York Harbor in 1886 in three hundred and fifty pieces, then was reassembled and dedicated in October of that year.

beats.poi_name: Ellis Island National Museum of Immigration
beats.script_body: The museum is housed in the old immigration building of 1900, and the moment you enter — greeted by stacks of luggage and photographs — you get a feel for what life was like for the new arrivals. On January 1, 1892, fifteen-year-old Annie Moore from Ireland became the very first immigrant to be inspected and have her details recorded here. Millions followed from all over Europe, their journeys driven by persecution, pogroms, and lack of work.

beats.script_body: Part of the Smithsonian Institution, this branch resides in the George Gustav Heye Center, which occupies two floors of the 1907 beaux arts Alexander Hamilton U.S. Custom House at the foot of Broadway. Nearby Bowling Green is reputedly where the Dutch made a deal for Manhattan Island with the Native American inhabitants.

beats.script_body: One of Manhattan's oldest buildings, this tavern was by the 1760s a popular meeting place for patriots known as the Sons of Liberty. Here, in 1783, George Washington bade farewell to the officers of the Continental Army. Today the site is a museum complex of four nineteenth-century buildings plus the tavern, which was reconstructed in 1907, with galleries of period paintings, re-creations of post-Revolutionary rooms that were once government offices, and more than two hundred flags.

beats.script_body: Federal Hall is all about George Washington and "firsts." The bronze statue on the front steps marks the spot where Washington was inaugurated as president in 1789. This was the first capitol building of the new nation, where the first U.S. Congress met, and it was also the original City Hall of New York. The current building — an early example of Greek Revival architecture — was finished in 1842, and the broad steps outside still offer a great view of the narrow historic streets of the nation's first capital.

beats.script_body: This historic church was founded by Anglicans in 1697 and destroyed twice — by fire in 1776 and after heavy snow in 1839. The current Gothic Revival church dates from 1846. You enter through bronze doors sculpted with Biblical scenes similar to those on the Baptistry in Florence, and inside the vaulted ceiling opens the narrow space up to a stained-glass wall above the altar. Among the congregation's prominent members was the Federalist Alexander Hamilton, who is buried in the churchyard.

beats.script_body: It would be impossible to imagine New York without its immigrant populations, visible in the Lower Manhattan enclaves of Little Italy and Chinatown. Every group that settled here — like the Italian stonemasons and Eastern European tailors of the nineteenth century — added to America's cultural heritage. The familiar "melting pot" term came from a 1908 play of the same name by the Anglo-Jewish activist and writer Israel Zangwill, though for New York it is somewhat misleading: the ethnic groups did not meld but clustered in neighborhoods that preserved their language, culture, food, and customs.

beats.source_passage: It would be impossible to imagine New York without its dynamic immigrant populations, visible, among other places, in the famous Lower Manhattan enclaves of Little Italy and Chinatown. Indeed, every group that has settled here, such as the Italian stonemasons and Eastern European tailors of the 19th century, has added to America's cultural heritage ... The familiar "melting pot" term came from a 1908 play of the same name by the Anglo-Jewish activist and writer, Israel Zangwill. ... The different ethnic groups that came to the city in the 19th and early 20th centuries did not meld, but clustered in neighborhoods that preserved their language, culture, food, and customs.

beats.script_body: The Bowery marks the beginning of the Lower East Side, once home to a thriving Jewish community and today known for its nightlife and hip hotels, where boutiques trade in vintage cool. You can appease kids with a trip to Economy Candy on Rivington Street for throwbacks like Jujubes and Whatchamacallit bars.

beats.script_body: Lower Manhattan technically takes in everything below Houston Street, between the Hudson and East Rivers, and its historic role founded New York City and turned it into a commercial power. At the tip of Manhattan, the Dutch purchased the island from the local Lenape people in 1626, and the city came under British control in 1664. Later, in 1785, New York became the first capital of the new nation following the Revolutionary War.

disputes.claim: New York became the first capital of the new nation in 1785
disputes.issue: Book says 1785; the First Federal Congress convened in NYC and Washington was inaugurated here in 1789. NYC served as the national capital 1785-1790 under the Articles of Confederation (Congress of the Confederation moved to NYC in 1785), so 1785 is defensible for 'capital' but ambiguous vs 1789 'first capital under the Constitution'. Not auto-corrected — date is source-faithful and arguably correct.

review_queue.description: Book says Battery Park 'Dutch settlers landed here in 1623' while the Lower Manhattan intro says the Dutch purchased the island in 1626. These are different events (settlement vs purchase) and not contradictory; both kept verbatim.
